Meyer, the Church Pulpit Commentary, and NET Bible notes. My searches for Catholic/Orthodox sources were cut short by tool limits. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

## Judges 15 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1
Samson returns after an interval ("after days," likely about a year) during the wheat harvest (May/June). He brings a young goat — a customary gift for reconciliation, as Judah brought to Tamar (Gen 38:17). His intent ("go in to my wife into the chamber") uses a Hebrew idiom with clear sexual connotations; he intends to consummate the marriage that was interrupted in ch. 14. The father blocks him. Gill notes that Samson could have forced his way in but chose restraint.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/15-1.htm

### v. 2
The father-in-law claims he "thoroughly thought" Samson hated his wife — the Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis ("saying, I said"). The Pulpit Commentary suggests this was a flimsy excuse: the father never informed Samson before giving his daughter to the "companion" (the best man from ch. 14). He then offers the younger sister instead. Bush (quoted at Precept Austin) notes this would have been an incestuous marriage under Leviticus 18:18, though the Philistines might not have regarded it so. Gill likewise observes Samson "listened not to the proposal" knowing it violated God's law.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/15-1.htm

### v. 3
Samson declares he will be "blameless" (or "innocent" / "justified," as the NET renders it) in harming the Philistines. Guzik notes that God used Samson's ungodly anger for His purposes, citing Psalm 76:10 — "Surely the wrath of man shall praise You" — yet this does not justify Samson's anger. Keil & Delitzsch (quoted at Precept Austin) argue Samson "acted rather in a public than a private capacity": the slight was put upon him *because he was an Israelite*, so he takes revenge as Israel's judge. Precept Austin observes a significant omission: the text does *not* say the Spirit of the Lord moved or empowered him for this act. This was personal resentment, not divine judgment.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary

### v. 4
Samson catches 300 foxes (or jackals — the Hebrew *shu'al* can refer to jackals, which run in packs of up to 200). Gill addresses objections: (a) Palestine abounded with foxes/jackals, (b) Samson may have employed others to help, (c) he need not have caught them all in one day, and (d) divine providence could easily gather them. Gill also notes some critics tried to re-translate "foxes" as "sheaves" of corn, but he rejects this as contrary to the Hebrew, the ancient versions, and Josephus. The tactic of tying pairs of foxes tail-to-tail with a torch between them ensured they could not run straight to their own dens but would zigzag, spreading fire widely.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary

### v. 5
The torches are lit and the foxes released into the "standing grain" (ripe wheat), burning shocks (cut sheaves), standing corn, vineyards, and olive groves. This caused massive economic damage. Gill notes that foxes, naturally terrified of fire at their tails, would run into the first shelter they found — the grain fields — spreading the fire. The Church Pulpit Commentary calls it "devastation … considerable" and notes it occurred about end of April when shocks lay on the fields awaiting the threshing floor. Guzik remarks Samson "seemed to act like a juvenile delinquent," yet God used it for His purposes.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary

### v. 6
The Philistines discover Samson was responsible. Ironically, they retaliate not against Samson but against his wife and her father — burning them to death, the very fate the woman had tried to avoid in ch. 14 by betraying Samson's riddle. Gill comments that "that evil came upon her she thought to avoid." The Pulpit Commentary notes the irony: those who occasioned the evil are punished, but by the Philistines themselves, not by Samson, and "one wrong leads to another."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/judges/15.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/

### v. 7
Samson vows revenge and says "after that I will cease." Guzik calls this "the bitter story of retaliation — of trying to avenge wrongs done to us." He contrasts it with Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:38-42. Gill, however, argues Samson's motivation was not merely private revenge: "what he did was not in a way of private revenge, but on account of the injury done to the people of Israel, he taking what was done to them as done to himself, the chief magistrate and judge of Israel." Precept Austin sides with the more critical view: Samson "was concerned only for personal vengeance and failed to understand his God-ordained role in the 'holy war' against Israel's enemies."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary

### v. 8
"He attacked them hip and thigh with a great slaughter" — a proverbial expression for an unsparing, brutal slaughter. Gill explains the Targum renders it "horse and foot" (cavalry and infantry), though Gill thinks this less likely. Samson then retreats to "the cleft of the rock of Etam," a cave in the territory of Judah. Guzik notes: "Samson had no more family and could trust virtually no one. He lived like a fugitive, alone in a cave."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/

### v. 9
The Philistines "went up" — from the coastal plain (Shephelah) to the hill country of Judah — and encamped at Lehi. Ellicott notes that Lehi is named by anticipation; it receives its name ("jawbone") from the event about to occur. The Pulpit Commentary identifies possible sites: Tell-el-Lekhiyeh (near Beersheba) or Beit-Likiyeh (in Wady Suleiman, near Beth-horon and Timnah), but says "no certainty can at present be arrived at."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/15-9.htm

### v. 10
The men of Judah ask the Philistines why they have come in force. The Philistines answer plainly: to arrest Samson and "do to him as he has done to us." Gill notes that Josephus records the men of Judah protesting they had paid their tribute and submitted quietly to Philistine rule.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html

### v. 11
Three thousand men of Judah go to Samson's cave. Their question — "Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us?" — exposes their accommodation to oppression. Guzik observes: "Samson didn't want to hear this or recognize it. As far as he was concerned, the Philistines should not rule over the people of God." The Pulpit Commentary notes the pathos: "Those who have received the greatest benefits often betray their benefactors … Christ by Judas, and rejected by the Jews." Samson answers: "As they did to me, so I have done to them" — a personal rather than national rationale. Constable contrasts Samson's "radical commitment with Judah's wretched compromise."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/judges/15.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary (Constable excerpt)

### vv. 12-13
Samson makes the men of Judah swear they will not kill him themselves. They bind him with "two new ropes" — not old, weak ones, but new, strong ones, and likely made of flax. Gill notes the care taken: two ropes rather than one, new rather than old, "for greater security." Guzik sees great faith in Samson's submission: "He was willing to put himself in a difficult position and to trust God to take care of him." Gill sees a typological parallel: Samson consented to be bound and delivered to his enemies, "which he was a type of Christ, who was betrayed by the Jews, and delivered by them into the hands of the Romans."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html

### v. 14
At Lehi, the Philistines shout in triumph — but "the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him." The ropes become "like flax that is burnt with fire" and melt from his hands. Gill says the Hebrew verb for "loosed" means "melted away" — like wax before fire or snow before sun. The Church Pulpit Commentary draws a devotional application: "Are there any … bound by evil habits, as by new cords? … Let them look up … and receive … the Holy Spirit; and … their bands shall drop off their hands, as flax touched by fire." Constable notes that the Spirit gave Samson his supernatural strength.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html

### v. 15
Samson finds a "fresh" (moist, still strong, not brittle) jawbone of a donkey and kills a thousand men. Gill notes the jawbone was providentially at hand; Jarchi suggests the word for "fresh" may carry overtones of the moist, purulent matter still on it, making it tougher. Constable compares this to Shamgar's exploit with an oxgoad (Judges 3:31) — an unlikely instrument proving more than adequate. The Pulpit Commentary draws a homiletic point: "Through God's blessing the grandest results have been produced by the rudest and simplest means … The preaching of the gospel by unlettered fishermen."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/

### v. 16
Samson's victory song is a Hebrew pun: "With the jawbone of a donkey (*chamor*), heaps upon heaps (*chamor chamoratayim*) — with the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men." The NET Bible notes several translation options: (a) "a heap, two heaps" (referring to corpses), (b) "I have made donkeys of them" (a denominative verb from "donkey"), (c) "I have thoroughly skinned them" (from an Arabic cognate), or (d) "I have stormed mightily against them" (from a verb meaning "to foam/boil up"). Moffatt rendered it: "With the jawbone of an ass, I have piled them in a mass." Constable notes Samson "loved riddles and rhymes."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/

### v. 17
He throws the jawbone away and names the place Ramath-lehi ("Jawbone Height" or "Jawbone Hill"). The Pulpit Commentary calls this "lifting up the jawbone" — a memorial to the victory. Constable suggests the hill may have been the mound of corpses itself.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/

### v. 18
Samson's first recorded prayer in the narrative. He is desperately thirsty and cries to the LORD. Significantly, he acknowledges God as the source of the victory: "You have given this great deliverance by the hand of Your servant." Constable notes that "the word translated 'you' is in the emphatic position in the Hebrew text" — Samson truly gives God the credit. Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) says: "It is very usual for God's people, when they have had some great deliverance, to have some little trouble that is too much for them. Samson slays a thousand Philistines … and then he must needs die for want of a little water!" Matthew Poole (also quoted by Guzik) suggests the thirst "was partly sent by God, that by the experience of his own impotency he might be forced to ascribe the victory to God only, and not to himself." The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary likewise says "Perhaps the Lord let Samson become so tired and extremely thirsty to remind him of the source of his strength."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-15.html (via Precept Austin)

### v. 19
God splits open "the hollow place" at Lehi and water gushes out. The Hebrew word for "hollow place" (*maktesh*) means a mortar-shaped cavity. Gill, citing Jarchi, says a tooth socket was knocked out and water flowed from it — a double miracle. However, the Church Pulpit Commentary and most modern translations clarify that God opened a hollow place *in Lehi* (the location), not in the jawbone itself — "the translation 'jaw' leaves the wrong impression, that the water flowed out of the jawbone." Samson revives and names the spring En-hakkore ("Spring of the Caller" or "Supplicant's Spring"). Spurgeon (in *The Fainting Hero*) draws a devotional parallel: the believer can look at "heaps upon heaps" of defeated enemies (sins, doubts, fears, sorrows), yet even after great victories, fresh challenges come — but "the past victory was a promise of future deliverance." F.B. Meyer is quoted: "Be of good courage, fainting warrior! The God who made thee, and has used thee, knows thy frame, and what thou needest before thou askest."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html

### v. 20
A summary statement: Samson judged Israel twenty years during the Philistine oppression. Constable notes this verse "separates his story into two parts" — the writer records Samson's acts that gradually increased in severity against the Philistines first (chs. 14–15), then the chain of events leading to his self-destruction (ch. 16). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary observes that Samson "could not deliver the Israelites from the Philistines" but did become their acknowledged judge. Notably, "Israel must never have repented and prayed to the Lord for deliverance" — a striking absence in the Samson cycle.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary (Constable excerpt)

## Traditions Compared

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)
Emphasises that God *used* Samson despite his ungodly anger and disobedience — "Surely the wrath of man shall praise You" (Ps 76:10). Samson is a cautionary tale: "how much more he might have accomplished had he been wholly yielded to God instead of governed by his own passions" (quoting G. Campbell Morgan). The jawbone sermon illustration (novel, convenient, simple, ridiculous, successful weapon) ties to gospel preaching. The miraculous provision of water illustrates that "God's work, done God's way, will always be provided for by God."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/

### Reformed Baptist (Gill; Spurgeon)
Gill reads Samson's motives more charitably: he acted "not in a way of private revenge, but on account of the injury done to the people of Israel … as the chief magistrate and judge of Israel." He also sees clear typology: Samson bound and delivered up prefigures Christ. Spurgeon (quoted in Guzik) focuses on Samson's "simple-minded faith" — "nothing but a big child" — turning to his heavenly Father in prayer, and on the pattern of post-victory weakness that drives the saint to dependence.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-15.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-15/

### Evangelical / Dispensational (Constable; NET Bible)
Constable sees Samson's confidence at Lehi as ambiguous: it could be remarkable faith, or it could be self-reliance — "I prefer the second explanation since it seems more consistent with Samson's character." He highlights the Hebrew wordplay and the literary structure (ch. 15 as the dividing point before Samson's downfall). The NET Bible offers modern text-critical notes on the difficult Hebrew of v. 16 and translates "foxes" as "jackals."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Ellicott's notes are briefer and focus on historical and linguistic details: the timing of wheat harvest (mid-May in the Shephelah), the meaning of the Hebrew idiom for "go in to my wife," and the identification of Lehi. He also remarks that "uxoriousness was the chief secret of the weakness and ruin of Samson, as it was afterwards of … Solomon."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/15-1.htm

### Holiness / Keswick (F.B. Meyer; Church Pulpit Commentary)
F.B. Meyer (Baptist with strong Holiness influence) emphasises God's faithfulness to the fainting warrior. The Church Pulpit Commentary stresses application to the believer's sanctification: "Every great deed and heroic uplifting of soul … is a Divine gift — a treasure in an earthen vessel." The thirst after victory teaches dependence: "The faith that made Samson irresistible in battle now makes him prevail with God."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/judges/15.htm

## Modern Scholarship (NET Bible Notes)

- **v. 1**: The Hebrew idiom "go to" (*bo' 'el*) has sexual connotations and is a cohortative form expressing resolve.
- **v. 4**: "Foxes" is rendered "jackals" — the Hebrew *shu'al* can refer to either, but jackals are known to run in large packs.
- **v. 16**: The phrase *chamor chamoratayim* is highly uncertain. Options include "a heap, two heaps" (corpses), "I have made donkeys of them," "I have thoroughly skinned them" (Arabic cognate), or "I have stormed mightily against them" (from *chamar*, "to foam/boil").
- **v. 19**: The "hollow place" (*maktesh*) is a geographical feature at Lehi, not in the jawbone itself — clarified as "the basin at Lehi."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_15_commentary (NET notes embedded)
